title: Prevenient Grace descending had remov'd The stonie from thir hearts
greek: Latin gratia praeveniens, 'grace that comes before'
short: God's grace 'comes before' human repentance and makes it possible: the stony heart is replaced by a heart of flesh, as in Ezekiel.
body: Adam and Eve's repentance is not their own achievement: 'Prevenient Grace descending had remov'd The stonie from thir hearts, and made new flesh Regenerat grow instead'. 'Prevenient' (Latin praevenire, 'to come before') names grace that precedes and enables any human turning to God; Verity cites the Prayer Book collect 'that thy grace may always prevent and follow us', and the image is from Ezekiel 11:19, 'I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh'. Their prayers, groaned 'unutterable' by the Spirit's prompting (Romans 8:26, as Verity notes), rise to Heaven, where the Son presents them as 'first fruits' of grace. The episode fulfils the Father's promise of 3.173-202 and answers Satan, for whom no such grace is offered.

title: th' ancient Pair In Fables old ... Deucalion and chaste Pyrrha ... the Shrine Of Themis
short: Adam and Eve at prayer are compared to the couple who survived the classical Flood and prayed at the shrine of Themis to restore mankind.
body: Adam and Eve's prayer is no less weighty than that of 'th' ancient Pair In Fables old, less ancient yet then these, Deucalion and chaste Pyrrha to restore The Race of Mankind drownd, before the Shrine Of Themis stood devout'. Verity explains that Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha were the only survivors of the Greek flood, who asked the oracle of Themis, goddess of law and right, how to renew the human race, and were told to throw 'the bones of their mother', stones, behind them (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.313-415). The Greek flood story was commonly treated as a version of Noah's flood, and Milton's 'Fables old, less ancient yet then these' again ranks myth below scriptural history. The comparison anticipates the vision of the Flood later in the book.

title: four faces each Had, like a double Janus ... the eyes of Argus
greek: Latin Ianus bifrons; Greek Argos Panoptês
short: Michael's cherubic guard have four faces, like a doubled two-faced Janus, and more eyes than hundred-eyed Argus, and cannot be lulled asleep.
body: Michael comes with a band of cherubim, each with 'four faces ... like a double Janus', their bodies spangled with eyes 'more numerous then those Of Argus, and more wakeful then to drouze, Charm'd with Arcadian Pipe, the Pastoral Reed Of Hermes, or his opiate Rod'. Verity explains: the four faces come from Ezekiel's cherubim (Ezekiel 1, 10); Janus, the Roman god of doorways, had two faces (Virgil's 'Ianique bifrontis imago', Aeneid 7.180), so four faces make 'a double Janus'. Argus, the hundred-eyed watchman set by Hera over Io, was lulled to sleep by Hermes' pipe and wand and killed (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.668-723). The cherubim are guardians who, unlike Argus or the angels of Book IV, cannot be beguiled. Janus is apt for a gatekeeper.

title: Leucothea wak'd
short: The dawn is personified as Leucothea, the 'white goddess', whom the Romans identified with Mater Matuta, goddess of the morning.
body: 'Mean while To resalute the World with sacred Light Leucothea wak'd'. Verity explains that the Greek sea-goddess Leucothea ('white' or 'bright goddess', the deified Ino) was identified by the Romans with Mater Matuta, goddess of the dawn, whom Lucretius describes ushering in the morning (5.656); Milton transfers the office to Leucothea. Ovid tells the story of Ino's transformation into Leucothea (Metamorphoses 4.416-562; Fasti 6.473-550). The dawn image is double-edged: it is the first morning after repentance, but also the day of expulsion. It contrasts with the rosy and joyful dawns of Book V, which woke Adam and Eve to work and praise in Paradise.

title: the Bird of Jove ... the Beast that reigns in Woods ... Hart and Hinde
short: The first sign of the fallen world: an eagle strikes two birds and a lion chases a hart and hind towards the eastern gate, prefiguring the expulsion.
body: Nature shows 'mute signs': the air darkens in eclipse, 'the Bird of Jove', the eagle, drives two 'Birds of gayest plume' before him, and the lion, 'the Beast that reigns in Woods', pursues 'A gentle brace, Goodliest of all the Forrest, Hart and Hinde', both pairs fleeing 'Direct to th' Eastern Gate'. Verity explains that the omens are symbolic: the two birds and two beasts represent the human pair, and their flight to the eastern gate foreshadows the banishment; he compares the eagle seizing a swan in Aeneid 12.247-56 and the twelve swans of Aeneid 1.393. The birds and beasts now prey on each other, a change already introduced in 10.707-14. Adam reads the signs with misgiving, 'Why in the East Darkness ere Dayes mid-course?'

title: Michael's dress: Livelier then Meliboean, or the graine Of Sarra
short: Michael comes not in his own shape but as a warrior in purple richer than the dyes of Meliboea or Tyre, his sword at his side.
body: Michael comes 'Not in his shape Celestial, but as Man Clad to meet Man', in a military vest of purple 'Livelier then Meliboean, or the graine Of Sarra, worn by Kings and Hero's old In time of Truce; Iris had dipt the wooff'. Verity glosses: Meliboea in Thessaly was famous for purple (Virgil, Aeneid 5.251; Lucretius 2.500), and Sarra was the old name of Tyre, whose shellfish dye was the most precious purple (Virgil, Georgics 2.506); Iris, goddess of the rainbow, had dyed the weave. The sword is the one that wounded Satan (6.320-34). Unlike the 'sociable' Raphael, Michael is 'solemn and sublime', and Adam does not go out to meet him. His name means 'who is like God?' (see 6.44).

anchor: Must I thus leave thee Paradise?
title: Must I thus leave thee Paradise? ... O flours
short: Eve's lament on hearing of the expulsion: she grieves for her native soil and the flowers she named and tended, and for the nuptial bower.
body: Overhearing the sentence, Eve cries: 'Must I thus leave thee Paradise? thus leave Thee Native Soile, these happie Walks and Shades'. Verity glosses 'Native', since Eve, unlike Adam, was created within Paradise (Genesis 2:7-8). She mourns her flowers, 'which I bred up with tender hand From the first op'ning bud, and gave ye Names', and the 'nuptial Bowre'. The Dartmouth edition notes her naming of the flowers, a counterpart to Adam's naming of the animals (8.343-56). Verity also hears an echo of the consolation that 'every place is a country to a wise man', as in Shakespeare's Richard II. Michael answers gently that 'where he abides, think there thy native soil' (11.292), a lesson completed in the last lines of the poem.

title: In the Visions of God: It was a Hill Of Paradise the highest
short: Michael leads Adam up the highest hill of Paradise to see the future, a scene paralleled by Satan's showing Christ the kingdoms of the world.
body: Michael leads Adam up 'In the Visions of God' (Ezekiel 40:2, 'In the visions of God brought he me ... upon a very high mountain', which Verity cites) to 'a Hill Of Paradise the highest, from whose top The Hemisphere of Earth in cleerest Ken Stretcht out to amplest reach of prospect lay'. It was 'Not higher' nor wider-viewing than the mountain on which 'the Tempter set Our second Adam in the Wilderness, To shew him all Earths Kingdomes and thir Glory' (Matthew 4:8). Verity notes that in Paradise Regained Milton places that temptation on a mountain usually identified with Niphates. The parallel sets the two Adams side by side: the first is shown history by an angel for instruction, the second is shown empires by Satan for temptation.

title: Cambalu, seat of Cathaian Can ... Samarchand ... Paquin ... Agra and Lahor
short: From the hill Adam's eye sweeps over the future empires of Asia, Africa and America, a catalogue of exotic capitals drawn from seventeenth-century geography.
body: The catalogue (11.388-411) surveys the world's future seats of power. Verity explains the Asian names: Cambalu, the capital of the 'Cathaian Can' (Khan), properly Khanbaliq, 'city of the Khan', built by Kublai Khan, which Milton, following old maps, treats as distinct from 'Paquin' (Peking); Samarkand on the Oxus, the throne of 'Temir' (Timur, Marlowe's Tamburlaine); Agra and Lahore of the 'great Mogul'; Ecbatana, Isfahan, Moscow and 'Bizance' (Constantinople). In Africa the names include the Negus of Abyssinia, Mombasa, Kilwa and Melinde, and Sofala 'thought Ophir'; in America, Montezuma's Mexico, Cuzco of 'Atabalipa' (Atahualpa) and 'yet unspoil'd Guiana', the supposed El Dorado. Verity compares Tasso's similar catalogue and notes Milton's sources in Heylyn and Mercator. The list is a survey of empire as the fallen world's ambition.

title: purg'd with Euphrasie and Rue The visual Nerve ... three drops from the Well of Life
short: Michael clears Adam's sight with eyebright and rue, herbs believed to cure dim eyes, and three drops from the well of life.
body: The false fruit 'that promis'd clearer sight' had bred a film on Adam's eyes; Michael removes it, 'then purg'd with Euphrasie and Rue The visual Nerve, for he had much to see; And from the Well of Life three drops instill'd'. Verity explains that euphrasy, 'eyebright', was used against dim sight because, by the doctrine of signatures, its eye-like flower showed its use, and that rue was also held to quicken the sight (Gerard's Herball). The well of life recalls Psalm 36:9, 'with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light'. Verity suggests that the blind Milton is thinking of his own eyes, which his nephew said he had damaged with remedies. The 'mental sight' that follows recalls the poet's prayer that light 'Shine inward' (3.51-55).

title: the first death: the Tiller and the Shepherd (Cain and Abel)
short: Adam's first vision is the murder of Abel by Cain, after God accepts the shepherd's sacrifice: the first death he sees is a brother's murder.
body: Michael shows a field where 'a sweatie Reaper' (Cain) brings a careless offering 'Uncull'd, as came to hand', while 'a Shepherd next' (Abel) offers 'The Firstlings of his Flock Choicest and best'; fire from heaven consumes Abel's sacrifice in sign of acceptance, and Cain kills him with a stone. Verity notes that Genesis 4:4 says only that God 'had respect unto Abel and to his offering', and that Milton follows the common interpretation by heavenly fire, as with the offerings of Gideon and Elijah. The names are never given, which makes the scene a type rather than a story. Adam's horror, 'But have I now seen Death?', shows the terrible newness of what the poem has so far only described, and Michael replies that this is only the first of many shapes of death.

title: A Lazar-house it seemd ... and over them triumphant Death his Dart Shook
short: A vision of a hospital filled with every disease; in 1674 Milton added three lines naming madness, melancholy and wasting sickness.
body: Michael shows 'A Lazar-house', a hospital for lepers (from Lazarus the beggar, Luke 16:20, as Verity notes), full of diseases: spasms, convulsions, epilepsies, catarrhs, stone and ulcers. Verity records that the second edition (1674) added three lines (11.485-87 in modern numbering): 'Daemoniac Phrenzie, moaping Melancholie And Moon-struck madness, pining Atrophie, Marasmus, and wide-wasting Pestilence'; in the text given here, which follows the first edition, they appear only in the variant notes at the end of the book. Newton reports that Pope admired them. 'And over them triumphant Death his Dart Shook, but delaid to strike, though oft invok't' (11.491-93 in 1674 numbering); Verity cites Tennyson's admiration of the strong monosyllable 'Shook' and the pause after it. The scene moves Adam to tears.

title: the sound Of Instruments that made melodious chime ... one who at the Forge
short: The descendants of Cain invent music and metal-working: Jubal, father of harp and organ, and Tubal-cain, the first smith (Genesis 4:21-22).
body: Adam sees tents and herds and hears 'the sound Of Instruments that made melodious chime', harp and organ, played by one whose 'volant touch Instinct through all proportions low and high Fled and pursu'd transverse the resonant fugue'. This is Jubal, 'the father of all such as handle the harp and organ' (Genesis 4:21). Verity notes that the organ was Milton's own instrument, which his father taught him, and that the description is a famous example of his exact use of musical terms such as 'fugue'. Next comes 'one who at the Forge' melts iron and brass, Tubal-cain, 'an instructor of every artificer in brass and iron' (Genesis 4:22), as Verity glosses. The arts are good in themselves, but practised by the race of Cain they become instruments of luxury and war.

title: A Beavie of fair Women ... the Sons of God ... Mans effeminate slackness
short: The pious men of the hills are seduced by the beautiful women of Cain's line; Milton reads Genesis 6:2's 'sons of God' as men, not angels.
body: From the hills come 'just men' who studied God's works; on the plain they see 'A Beavie of fair Women, richly gay In Gems and wanton dress', who sing and dance, and the men are caught 'in the amorous Net'. The scene interprets Genesis 6:2, 'the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair'. Verity explains that Milton, following Josephus and a widespread interpretation (Newton), takes the 'sons of God' as the descendants of Seth, who lived near Paradise and studied the heavens, and the women as Cain's descendants; elsewhere (5.447; Paradise Regained 2.178-79) he alludes to the alternative reading that they were angels. Michael's comment, that 'Mans woe' begins 'From Mans effeminate slackness' (11.632-33 in 1674 numbering), Verity takes as Milton's own opinion.

title: Giants of mightie Bone ... one rising, eminent
short: A vision of war among the giants born of these marriages, modelled on the shield of Achilles; one just man, Enoch, rises to speak and is rescued by God.
body: The next scene shows cities, war and siege: 'Giants of mightie Bone, and bould emprise', the 'mighty men which were of old, men of renown' of Genesis 6:4. Verity observes that the whole picture (11.638-73) is modelled on the city at war and the city at peace on the shield of Achilles (Iliad 18.478-608) and on Virgil's shield of Aeneas (Aeneid 8.608-731). In the council 'one rising, eminent In wise deport', Enoch, 'the seventh from thee' (11.700 in 1674 numbering), speaks of right and justice and is about to be killed when 'a Cloud descending snatch'd him thence' (Genesis 5:24; Jude 14-15), as Verity notes. Verity also reports Todd's view that 'sword-law' glances at Hobbes. Enoch is a type of the solitary witness, like Abdiel.

title: The one just Man alive: Noah and the Ark
short: Noah, a 'Reverend Sire' who preaches righteousness to a corrupt world, builds the Ark at God's command and survives the Flood.
body: After a vision of luxury and corruption, a 'Reverend Sire' (Noah) preaches 'Conversion and Repentance' in vain (1 Peter 3:19-20; 2 Peter 2:5, 'Noah ... a preacher of righteousness'); Verity notes that Milton follows Josephus' Antiquities in some details and that he once listed 'The Flood' as a subject for tragedy. Noah builds 'a wondrous Ark' and 'The one just Man alive' is saved with his family and the animals 'by sevens, and pairs' (Genesis 6-7). Verity notes echoes of Ovid's flood, 'sea without shore' recalling 'deerant quoque litora ponto' (Metamorphoses 1.292). Noah repeats the pattern of the poem's heroes: one man faithful among the faithless, like Abdiel and Enoch.

title: pushd by the horned floud ... an Iland salt and bare, The haunt of Seales and Orcs
short: The Flood will sweep the mount of Paradise down the river into the Persian Gulf as a barren island: God gives no holiness to place.
body: Michael foretells that the mount of Paradise will be 'Mov'd out of his place, pushd by the horned floud, With all his verdure spoil'd, and Trees adrift Down the great River to the op'ning Gulf, And there take root an Iland salt and bare, The haunt of Seales and Orcs, and Sea-mews clang'. Verity explains 'horned' as branching into channels, like Horace's bull-shaped river Aufidus, and identifies the river as the Euphrates and the gulf as the Persian Gulf; 'orcs' are a kind of whale. He notes that the obliteration of Paradise by the Flood was a common belief, but that this particular explanation seems Milton's invention. The moral follows: 'God attributes to place No sanctitie, if none be thither brought By Men who there frequent', a Protestant rejection of holy places.

title: An Olive leafe he brings, pacific signe ... the Bow ... Cov'nant new
short: The dove's olive leaf and the rainbow, sign of God's covenant with Noah never to destroy the earth again by water, end the first day of visions.
body: The raven flies out of the Ark and does not return; the dove is sent twice and brings back 'An Olive leafe ... pacific signe' (Genesis 8:6-11). Verity notes that in Genesis the dove is feminine. Then a 'dewie Cloud' appears, with 'a Bow Conspicuous with three listed colours gay, Betok'ning peace from God, and Cov'nant new' (Genesis 9:11-17); Verity explains 'three' colours as the red, yellow and blue of the old theory of the rainbow, and quotes Dante's reference to the compact with Noah (Paradiso 12.17-18). Adam rejoices that God has not wholly abolished mankind, and Michael promises that 'Day and Night, Seed time and Harvest, Heat and hoary Frost' will continue until the final fire (Genesis 8:22). Book XI ends here; in 1667 the narrative continued without a break into the present Book XII.
